question.prompt: For how many positive integers \(n\) less than or equal to \(24\) is \(n!\) evenly divisible by \(1 + 2 + \cdots + n?\)

solutions.explanation:
First simplify the quotient we want to be an integer. Pairing the first and last terms gives \(1+2+\cdots+n=n(n+1)/2\), so
\[
\frac{n!}{1+2+\cdots+n}
=\frac{2(n-1)!}{n+1}.
\]
Here \(0!=1\), so the formula also includes \(n=1\). Put \(k=n+1\). We must count the integers \(2\le k\le25\) for which \(k\) divides \(2(k-2)!\).

If \(k=2\), the quotient is \(1\), so it works. If \(k\ge4\) is even, then \(k/2\le k-2\). Thus \(k/2\) is one of the factors in \((k-2)!\), and the extra factor \(2\) supplies a factor of \(k\). All \(12\) even values \(2,4,\ldots,24\) work.

If \(k\) is an odd prime, it cannot divide \(2(k-2)!\): none of the factors \(2,1,2,\ldots,k-2\) has prime factor \(k\).

It remains to check odd composites. An odd composite at most \(25\) has a smaller factor at most \(5\), so listing odd factor pairs gives exactly \(9,15,21,25\). All four work:

For \(k=9\), the factorial \(7!\) contains the distinct factors \(3\) and \(6\), whose product is divisible by \(9\).

For \(k=15\) and \(k=21\), use the distinct factors \(3,5\) in \(13!\) and \(3,7\) in \(19!\), respectively.

For \(k=25\), the factorial \(23!\) contains \(5\) and \(10\), whose product is divisible by \(25\).

These even, odd-prime, and odd-composite cases exhaust \(2\le k\le25\) without overlap. Exactly \(12+4=16\) values work, and each corresponds to one \(n=k-1\). The answer is \(16\), choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
